newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm ministers attack planned cereal cuts.
newsitem.headline: EU farm ministers attack planned cereal cuts.

text.p: European Union farm ministers attacked on Tuesday a proposal to cut direct aid payments to cereals farmers by 1.4 billion ecus ($1.6 billion) to fund extra aid for beef farmers hit by the mad cow crisis.

Opening a televised debate, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said that the cereals cuts, which were attached to a proposal for unchanged farm prices in the next marketing year starting in July, were needed to curb surging output.
But ministers protested that the payments, agreed in 1992 to compensate farmers for price and production cutting reforms, were permanent and could not be reduced.

"Any decrease would break the trust of our farmers. I reject this proposal with all due force," German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert said, firing the first broadside in a battle likely to last several months.
Fischler argued that cereals farmers were over-compensated and that the reforms permitted payments to be adjusted to take account of production and market trends.

French Farm Minister Philippe Vasseur said the pricing package, especially the cereal cuts, was unacceptable. "The reduction undermines the balance of the 1992 reforms and is incomprehensible," he said.

Fischler stressed that cereals output had to be curbed after surging 15 percent to a record 202 million tonnes in 1996 with a further increase expected this year after farmers were allowed to increase sowings.
Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates said that a cut in cereals aids was unjustified as record output had depressed prices considerably since last year and a further fall was expected.

Belgian Farm Minister Karel Pinxten said that cereals farmers should not have to pay for problems in the beef sector. "It's unacceptable to solve budgetary problems by transferring funds from one sector to another," he said.
Several ministers urged Fischler to propose as quickly as possible how much land cereals farmers must set aside for the 1998 harvest in order to qualify for EU subsidies.
Ministers are worried that in view of rising production, the current rate of five percent is likely to be greatly increased.
"It's really crucial to have a decision on set-aside in the prices package, especially if there is any change," France's Vasseur said.

Portuguese Farm Minister Fernando Gomes da Silva said that Portuguese cereals and oilseed farmers had suffered losses of up to 45 percent, the biggest since the Common Agricultural Policy was set up in 1962.
A number of ministers also attacked plans to reduce cereals and sugar aids to take account of lower interest rates.
Amid the traditional chorus of discontent, Sweden, Britain and Denmark struck discordant notes.
Sweden's Annika Ahnberg called for a general lowering of farm prices and increase in set-aside to meet future challenges of EU expansion eastwards and world trade liberalisation.
